title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera in 1975 and Still Went Bankrupt
alt_title_1: Steven Sasson's 8-Pound Prototype & The Cost of Protecting Old Margins
alt_title_2: Why Refusing to Cannibalize Yourself Hands Your Market to Outsiders
description_hook: In December 1975, 24-year-old Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built the world's first 8-pound digital camera (U.S. Patent 4,131,919). Fearful of cannibalizing high-margin chemical film that peaked near $16 billion in 1996, Kodak hesitated until filing Chapter 11 bankruptcy on January 19, 2012.

scenes.headline: Kodak Built the First Digital Camera in December 1975
scenes.stat_label: STEVEN SASSON'S 8-POUND DIGITAL PROTOTYPE AT KODAK
bullets: 24-year-old Kodak engineer captured filmless images onto tape
Awarded U.S. Patent 4,131,919 decades before smartphones
scenes.narration: Eastman Kodak did not miss the digital photography wave; a twenty-four-year-old Kodak electrical engineer named Steven Sasson built the world's first working eight-pound digital camera in December 1975.
scenes.source: U.S. Patent 4,131,919 (1978); Eastman Kodak Chapter 11 SDNY (Jan 19, 2012)

scenes.headline: Protected $16B Film Margins Until 2012 Bankruptcy
scenes.stat_label: CHAPTER 11 FILING AFTER SHIELDING LEGACY CHEMICAL FILM
bullets: Patented digital tech (4,131,919) yet feared hurting film profits
Revenue peaked near $16B (1996) -> Chapter 11 on Jan 19, 2012
scenes.narration: Sasson's camera earned U.S. Patent 4,131,919, yet executives feared cannibalizing lucrative chemical film. Kodak revenue peaked near sixteen billion dollars in 1996 before digital rivals crushed it into Chapter 11 bankruptcy on January 19, 2012.
scenes.source: U.S. Patent 4,131,919 (1978); Eastman Kodak Chapter 11 SDNY (Jan 19, 2012)

scenes.headline: Refusing to Cannibalize Never Stops the Future
scenes.left_body: Shelters legacy cash cow -> outsiders capture 100% of new era
scenes.right_body: Trades old margin voluntarily -> owns the next 20-year platform
scenes.narration: Locking a breakthrough inside a corporate drawer never halts technological shifts; protecting yesterday's comfortable margin only guarantees that hungry outsiders collect tomorrow's entire market instead of you.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule based on Kodak Chapter 11 Filing (2012)

scenes.headline: Automate Your Own Billable Workflow Before Rivals Do
scenes.stat_subtext: Automate manual hours first -> shift pricing from time to outcomes
scenes.narration: Run an annual self-disruption check on your career and solo business: whenever new software automates half of what clients pay you hourly to do, adopt it first and charge for outcomes.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin protocol (advice, not a study)

scenes.headline: Disrupt Your Cash Cow on Your Own Schedule
scenes.stat_label: OBSOLETE YOUR OLD WORKFLOW BEFORE A STRANGER DOES
bullets: Ask every January: how would a smart newcomer replace me?
Build that leaner offer yourself while cashflow is strong
scenes.narration: Cannibalize your own outdated workflow on your own terms today, before a hungrier competitor replaces your best margin for free.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule based on U.S. Patent 4,131,919 (1978)
